'''Bewdley''' ({{IPAc-en|audio=Bewdley pronunciation.ogg|ˈ|b|juː|d|l|i}} {{respell|BEWD|lee}}) is a town and [[Civil parishes in England|civil parish]] in the [[Wyre Forest District]] in [[Worcestershire]], England, on the banks of the [[River Severn]]. It is in the [[Severn Valley (England)|Severn Valley]], and is {{convert|3+1/2|mi|km|round=0.5|abbr=off}} west of [[Kidderminster]], {{convert|12+1/2|mi|km|0|abbr=on}} north of [[Worcester, England|Worcester]] and {{convert|23|mi|km|abbr=on}} southwest of [[Birmingham]]. It lies on the [[River Severn]], at the gateway of the [[Wyre Forest]] national nature reserve, and at the time of the [[2021 United Kingdom census|2021 census]] had a population of 9,267.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bewdley (Parish, United Kingdom) - Population Statistics, Charts, Map and Location |url=https://citypopulation.de/en/uk/westmidlands/admin/wyre_forest/E04010446__bewdley/ |access-date=2024-09-01 |website=citypopulation.de}}</ref> Bewdley is a popular tourist destination and is known for the [[Bewdley Bridge]], designed by [[Thomas Telford]], and the well-preserved [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] riverside.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.engineering-timelines.com/scripts/engineeringItem.asp?id=317 |title=Bewdley Bridge |website=Engineering Timelines |access-date=24 January 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110710193837/http://www.engineering-timelines.com/scripts/engineeringItem.asp?id=317 |archive-date=10 July 2011}}</ref>

==Town geography==
[[File:Bewdley and surroundings OS Vector Map District raster.png|thumb|left|Bewdley and surrounding area (Ordnance Survey)]]
Bewdley is a town in [[Worcestershire]], it is situated on the western bank of the [[River Severn]]. It lies within the [[Wyre Forest District]], but close to the boundary of the [[Malvern Hills District]], just 2 miles south of Bewdley. 

The surrounding landscape includes notable hill ranges, the [[Malvern Hills]] lie 11 miles to the south, the [[Shropshire Hills]] 12 miles to the west, and the [[Cotswolds]] 21 miles to the south east. 

Nearby towns include [[Stourport-on-Severn]] 2.5 miles to the south east, [[Kidderminster]] 3.5 miles to the East, and [[Worcester, England|Worcester]] just 12.5 miles to the south. 

[[File:Bewdleyskyline .jpg|left|thumb|Bewdley from the racks, 2019]]

Beyond the church, High Street leads off to the south towards [[Stourport-on-Severn|Stourport]] along the B4194, a road known locally as "the [[Hairpin turn|switchback]]" because of its many sharp curves. Unlike in many English towns, High Street is so called not because of its importance to commerce, but because of its geographical position 'high' above the river.

On the west side of the church, the B4190, named Welch Gate within town limits (so called because it once contained a [[tollgate]] on the road towards Wales), climbs steeply up to the west, giving access to the south side of the [[Wyre Forest]]. Dowles Road, a continuation of the B4194, leads northwest to [[Button Oak]], along the east and northeast side of the Wyre Forest. To the northeast of the town is the wooded hilltop of Wassel Wood in Trimpley, the southern terminus of [[Shatterford Hill]].

In the area between [[Stourport-on-Severn|Stourport]] and Bewdley are several large [[English country houses|country houses]]. [[Witley Court]], [[Astley Hall (Stourport-on-Severn)|Astley Hall]], and [[Pool House, Worcestershire|Pool House]] are considered particularly significant.

==History==
{{see also|History of Worcestershire}}
[[File:Bewdley Guildhall.jpg|thumb|left|[[Bewdley Guildhall]]]]
[[Mesolithic]]-period settlers have been identified through excavations in Wribbenhall, which found 1,400 fragments of flint tools, as well as post holes, a hearth, gullies and a pit. This site has been dated to roughly 6,800 BC, making it the oldest settlement yet identified in Worcestershire. Pollen evidence shows that crops were already being grown and woodlands cleared at this time.<ref>{{harvnb|Pevsner|Brookes|2007|pp=10–11}}</ref>

The main part of Bewdley town is situated on the western bank of the [[River Severn]], including the main street—Load Street. Its name derives from ''lode'', an old word for [[ferry]]. Load Street is notable for its width: it once also served as the town's [[market place]].

Most of Bewdley's shops and amenities are situated along Load Street, at the top of which lies [[Saint Anne|St Anne]]'s Church, built between 1745 and 1748 by Doctor Thomas Woodward of [[Chipping Campden]].

The settlement of Wribbenhall, on the eastern side of the Severn, and now part of Bewdley, was recorded in the ''[[Domesday Book]]'' as being part of the [[manorialism|manor]] of [[Kidderminster]]. By the 14th century, the town had come to be known as ''Beau lieu'', French for "Beautiful place". Two centuries later [[John Leland (antiquary)|John Leland]] wrote in his ''Itinerary'' that "a man cannot wish to see a towne<!--sic--> better".

Bewdley was granted [[borough]] status, as well as a weekly market, by [[Edward IV of England|King Edward IV]] in 1472. It retained this status until the local government reorganisation in 1974. A parliamentary report of 1777 listed Bewdley as having a [[parish]] [[workhouse]] accommodating up to 80 inmates.

Samuel Kenrick (1728–1811) moved to Bewdley in 1765 and lived there as a banker for the rest of his life. Throughout that time he wrote lengthy letters to his old Glasgow University friend, Rev. James Wodrow, minister in Stevenston, Ayrshire. Their correspondence contains many insights into life in late eighteenth-century Bewdley. For example, Kenrick described one of the annual visits to the town by the Methodist preacher, Rev. [[John Wesley]], who "has a little flock in this town whom he statedly visits in his regular excursions …. Sometimes he comes accompanied with the noise & parade of half a score horsemen, preceding his chariot, who set our whole streets in a gaze …. His friends consist of serious well disposed people of all denominations, who go under the name of Methodists." (Samuel Kenrick to James Wodrow, 20 March 1786).<ref>{{cite book|url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-wodrow-kenrick-correspondence-1750-1810-9780198809012?cc=au&lang=en&|title=The Wodrow-Kenrick Correspondence 1750-1810: Volume I: 1750-1783|date=2020-08-20|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-880901-2|editor-last=Fitzpatrick|editor-first=Martin|location=Oxford / New York|pages=68|editor-last2=Macleod|editor-first2=Emma|editor-last3=Page|editor-first3=Anthony}}</ref>

The [[borough]] had a population of 7,458 in 1841.<ref>''The National Cyclopaedia of Useful Knowledge'' Vol III, (1847) London, Charles Knight, p.281.</ref>

During the [[Second World War]], [[Ribbesford House]] in Bewdley was used as the headquarters for the [[Free French Forces|Free French]] officer cadets. The cadets consisted of 200 teenagers who undertook military training at Ribbesford House until they joined with other allied forces in the [[D Day]] invasion.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.birminghampost.co.uk/lifestyle/european-royalty-who-found-midlands-3940328 |title=The European royalty who found a Midlands home during World War Two |last1=Upton |first1=Chris |date=25 September 2009 |newspaper=[[Birmingham Post]] |access-date=3 October 2013}}</ref>

The former [[quay]]side on the western bank of the river has been much upgraded and landscaped over the last few decades. Its rows of [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] [[townhouse]]s and buildings are well seen from [[Thomas Telford|Telford]]'s bridge. Since the completion of the flood defences in 2006 (see below), a "Civic Space" has been introduced to replace the old [[bandstand]]. It is used on a variety of occasions, including the twice monthly Bewdley Riverside Market.

==Governance==
Bewdley is now governed by three tiers of local government, in increasing order of size: Bewdley [[town council]], [[Wyre Forest (district)|Wyre Forest]] [[Districts of England|district council]], and Worcestershire [[county council]].

For many centuries Bewdley had its own [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP), most notably [[Stanley Baldwin]], who served as the Conservative Prime Minister, who represented it from 1908 to 1937. Reflecting changes in population, in 1950 the [[Bewdley (UK Parliament constituency)|Bewdley constituency]] was abolished, and the town was included in the [[Kidderminster (UK Parliament constituency)|Kidderminster constituency]].

In 1983, the Kidderminster constituency (including Bewdley) was absorbed into the [[Wyre Forest (UK Parliament constituency)|Wyre Forest constituency]]. The MP for Wyre Forest is [[Mark Garnier]] of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], who in 2010 unseated the incumbent, [[Richard Taylor (UK politician)|Richard Taylor]] of [[Independent Kidderminster Hospital and Health Concern]] (often simply ''Health Concern''), a local organisation. The Labour Party held the seat from 1997 to 2001.

==River and bridges==
[[File:Bewdley-bridge-town.jpg|thumb|right|[[Bewdley Bridge]] and Severn Side South, 2003]]

The [[River Severn]] often used to flood in winter, damaging many houses and commercial premises in Bewdley.  Among the worst floods in living memory were those in 1947, 1968 and 2000, where 140 properties were affected but after the 2000 floods, plans were made for flood defences on the western bank, completed in April 2006, costing £7 million.<ref name="test">{{cite web |url=http://www.geography.org.uk/resources/flooding/bewdley/flooddefencescheme |title=Bewdley Case Study: The Bewdley Flood Defence Scheme |website=[[Geographical Association]] |access-date=12 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160606135421/http://www.geography.org.uk/resources/flooding/bewdley/flooddefencescheme |archive-date=6 June 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Temporary barriers are also put up to protect properties on the eastern side of the river in Wribbenhall (on Beales Corner). In October 2023 work began on permanent flood defences for Beales Corner on the eastern bank, scheduled for completion in Autumn 2025. These necessitated the introduction of a temporary one-way traffic system over the bridge, meaning Bewdley Bridge would only be traversable by road traffic from east to west for most of the duration of the flood works. Bewdley's long experience of dealing with flooding resulted in the [[National Flood Forum]] being held in the town in 2002.

[[Bewdley Bridge]] over the Severn was built in 1798 by [[Thomas Telford]]. It was erected to replace the 1483 [[medieval]] bridge that was swept away in the floods of 1795. A modern road bridge, opened to the southeast of the town at Blackstone in 1987 after many decades of campaigning, carries the Bewdley bypass across the river.

The [[Tenbury and Bewdley Railway]] branched off the [[Severn Valley Railway]] at Bewdley, and ran through the Wyre Forest to [[Tenbury Wells]]. It crossed the river at [[Dowles]], over a bridge designed by William Clarke,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dowles Bridge - SVR Wiki |url=https://www.svrwiki.com/Dowles_Bridge |access-date=2024-04-18 |website=www.svrwiki.com}}</ref> a little to the north of Bewdley. This bridge was abandoned and dismantled in 1965, although its imposing brick and stone pillars remain. It was originally opened 100 years earlier, in August 1865.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Severn Bridges Demolished|url=https://www.severntales.co.uk/severnbridgesdemolished.html|access-date=2021-12-29|website=www.severntales.co.uk}}</ref>

==Education==

Three [[state school]]s are located in Bewdley. Of these, two are [[primary school]]s: St Anne's [[Church of England|CE]] Primary School on the west side of town and Bewdley Primary School in Wribbenhall on the eastern side of the Severn. Both were founded in 2007 when the region returned to a two-tier education system, replacing the former first and middle schools.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/116653|title=Bewdley, Wribbenhall First School|date=2019-11-29|access-date=2020-08-02|website=UK Government }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/135076|title=Bewdley Primary School|date=2020-07-24|access-date=2020-08-02|website=UK Government }}</ref>

The single [[secondary school]] is [[The Bewdley School]].

The Bewdley Grammar School on Lax Lane closed in the 1800s. Since then, the former grammar school has been adapted for many art galleries and art and craft activities. After the closure of Bewdley Grammar School, Bewdley High School & Sixth Form Centre was built on the opposite side of the river with new buildings. In 2007, Bewdley High School closed after 54 years due to an educational tier change that reorganised education as primary and secondary schools. All high schools were being replaced by new secondary schools.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kidderminstershuttle.co.uk/news/1554813.wyre-forest-schools-shake-up/|title=Wyre Forest schools shake-up|website=Kidderminster Shuttle|access-date=24 May 2019}}</ref>

In 2007, after new construction, landscaping, building refurbishments and extensions, [[The Bewdley School]] opened as a new secondary school. It provides facilities for the arts, science and outdoor learning to students.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.tes.com/jobs/employer/the-bewdley-school-and-sixth-form-centre-1010924|title=The Bewdley School and Sixth Form Centre - Tes Jobs|access-date=26 March 2021|archive-date=13 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613075245/https://www.tes.com/jobs/employer/the-bewdley-school-and-sixth-form-centre-1010924|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Bewdley Sixth Form is also part of [[The Bewdley School]], collectively offering GCSE and A Level courses.

In 2019, [[The Bewdley School]] won 'Secondary School of the Year' at the Worcestershire Educational Awards.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.worcesternews.co.uk/news/17735949.wea-2019-secondary-school-year-winner-goes-extra-mile|title=WEA 2019: Secondary School of the Year winner goes that 'extra mile'}}</ref>

==Media==
Local news and television programmes are provided by [[BBC West Midlands]] and [[ITV Central]]. Television signals are received from the [[Sutton Coldfield transmitting station|Sutton Coldfield]] TV transmitter <ref>{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/Sutton_Coldfield|title=Sutton Coldfield (Birmingham, England) Full Freeview transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|accessdate=23 January 2024}}</ref> and the local relay transmitter situated in [[Kidderminster]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/Kidderminster|title=Freeview Light on the Kidderminster (Worcestershire, England) transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|accessdate=23 January 2024}}</ref>

Local radio stations are [[BBC Hereford and Worcester]], [[Heart West Midlands]], [[Radio Wyvern]], [[Capital Mid-Counties]], [[Greatest Hits Radio|Greatest Hits Radio Herefordshire & Worcestershire]], [[Hits Radio Herefordshire & Worcestershire]], [[Smooth West Midlands]] and, previously, [[The Wyre]], a community based station.

The town is served by the local newspapers, ''[[The Shuttle (newspaper)|The Shuttle]]''.,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.kidderminstershuttle.co.uk |publisher=Kidderminster Shuttle |title=The Shuttle |access-date=23 January 2024}}</ref> Kidderminster Standard and ''[[Express & Star]]''.

==Local attractions==
[[File:Bewdley Railway Station 2017.jpg|thumb|left|Bewdley Station, now restored as part of the [[Severn Valley Railway]] ]]

===Events===
Bewdley also hosts one of the largest inland river [[regatta]]s in the country. The Bewdley [[Beer Festival]] is held each August Bank Holiday weekend. Bewdley also has an annual [[carnival]] which takes place every June. The Bewdley Festival, featuring a variety of artistic performances, is held annually in the town each October.

===Country music scene and festivals===
Bewdley has a distinguished music scene. It is particularly well known for its intimate [[country music]] venues and its many local festivals including the One Earth Festival, Bewdley music festival, Arley festival, and Bewdley Live.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bewdleylive.co.uk/ |title=Home |website=Bewdley Live |access-date=12 November 2017 |archive-date=18 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220818074135/http://bewdleylive.co.uk/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hopfest.co.uk/|title=Hopfest on Fire, Live Music |website=Hopfest |access-date=12 November 2017}}</ref> Former [[Led Zeppelin]] lead, and now solo singer, [[Robert Plant]] lives in the nearby village of [[Upper Arley]], and has been known to perform in the River Rooms; a small, intimate [[country music]] venue above the Cock and Magpie pub on the north riverside. The River Rooms attract country, soul, rock, jazz and pop performers from all across [[Europe]] and [[North America]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thecockandmagpie.com/live-music-events |title=Live music events |website=The Cock & Magpie, Bewdley |access-date=12 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161101132810/http://thecockandmagpie.com/live-music-events |archive-date=1 November 2016 |url-status=usurped}}</ref> Bewdley remains a significant centre for country music within the [[United Kingdom]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ents24.com/hub/search/near/Bewdley/genre/music |title=Bewdley |website=Ents24 |access-date=12 November 2017 |archive-date=26 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160826144441/https://www.ents24.com/hub/search/near/Bewdley/genre/music |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Other amenities===
The [[West Midlands Safari Park]] is located nearby on the [[A456 road|A456]] towards Kidderminster.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britishzoos.co.uk/westmidlandsafaripark/|title=West Midland Safari Park|work=britishzoos.co.uk|publisher=Diamond Publishing Ltd.|access-date=30 December 2012|archive-date=16 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131216184555/http://britishzoos.co.uk/westmidlandsafaripark/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Until the office moved in 2014 to Kidderminster, Bewdley contained the headquarters of the [[Severn Valley Railway]]. This [[heritage railway]] runs the {{convert|16|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} between [[Kidderminster]] and [[Bridgnorth]]. Bewdley remains the principal intermediate station on the line.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.svr.co.uk/visit-us/bewdley-station/|title=Bewdley Station|publisher= Severn Valley Railway |access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref>

The Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Gardens (usually abbreviated to simply "Jubilee Gardens") are located just off the High Street.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.greenflagaward.org/park-summary/?park=116|title=Queen Elizabeth II Silver Jubilee Gardens|publisher=Green Flag Award|access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref>

Bewdley is on the southeastern edge of the [[Wyre Forest]], and there are many footpaths and cycle routes through the woodlands. A visitor centre is situated just outside Bewdley at Callow Hill on the road to [[Cleobury Mortimer]], the head of many waymarked trails through the forest.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.countrysidemobility.org/locations/wyre-forest-park|title= Wyre Forest Park|publisher=Countryside Mobility|access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref> [[Knowles Mill]], a former corn mill owned by the National Trust is located within the forest.<ref>{{cite web |title=Knowles Mill |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/knowles-mill |access-date=29 July 2022 |website=National Trust}}</ref>

The [[Bewdley Museum]] explores the history of the town and surrounding areas; it is located in the former butchers' shambles just behind [[Bewdley Guildhall]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Bewdley Museum |url=https://www.discoverworcestershire.co.uk/listing/bewdley-museum/ |publisher=Discover Worcestershire |access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref>

Just outside Bewdley is Beaucastle, a Victorian mock-Gothic house, built in 1877. It was developed by George Baker, an industrialist and former Mayor of Birmingham and Bewdley. Beaucastle was designed by [[John Ruskin]] and William Doubleday.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.parksandgardens.org/places/beaucastle|title=Beaucastle |publisher=Parks and Gardens |access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref>

==Notable residents==
[[File:Bewdley Bridge from Severnside North.jpg|thumb|[[Bewdley Bridge]]]]
*[[Stanley Baldwin]], who served as prime minister three times between 1923 and 1937, was born at Lower Park House, Lower Park, in 1867. He served as [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|MP]] for the [[Bewdley (UK Parliament constituency)|town]] from 1908 for nearly thirty years and, in 1937, became ''[[Earl Baldwin of Bewdley]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.number10.gov.uk/history-and-tour/stanley-baldwin-2/ |title=Stanley Baldwin |access-date=31 July 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111216134952/http://www.number10.gov.uk/history-and-tour/stanley-baldwin-2/ |archive-date=16 December 2011}}</ref>
*[[Pamela Ball]], surgeon and local resident.<ref name="Macclesfield-1981">{{cite news |title=Foundations for romance |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/macclesfield-express/195213361/ |access-date=9 April 2026 |work=Macclesfield Express |date=September 3, 1981 |page=9}}</ref>
*[[John Beddoe]], [[ethnology|ethnologist]], was born in Bewdley in 1826.<ref>{{cite DNB12|wstitle=Beddoe, John|noicon=1|last=James|first=TE}}</ref>
* [[Jannion Steele Elliott]] (1871–1942), ornithologist and naturalist, lived at Dowles Manor from 1903 until his death.
*[[Alun Evans]], footballer, who in 1968 became the most expensive teenage transfer in history, moving from [[Wolverhampton Wanderers]] to [[Liverpool F.C.]], was born in the town.
*[[Becky Hill]], singer.
*Will Holland ([[Quantic (musician)|Quantic]]), musician, DJ and record producer, is from Bewdley.
*[[Karl Hyde]], musician, best known as a member of British [[techno]]/[[electronic music]] band [[Underworld (band)|Underworld]] was born in Bewdley.<ref>{{cite book |title=I am Dogboy |last=Hyde |first=Karl |publisher=Faber & Faber |year=2016 |isbn=978-0-571-32865-9 |location=London |pages=5}}</ref>
*[[Brian Turner Tom Lawrence]], awarded the [[Victoria Cross]] in the [[Boer War]], was born in Bewdley.
*[[Rustie Lee]], television chef and actress has lived in the town and local area for 20 years.
*[[Alison Mardell]], solicitor and senior Royal Air Force officer, was born here.
* Former [[Led Zeppelin]] lead- and now solo singer [[Robert Plant]] lives in the nearby village of [[Shatterford]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2015/02/07/whole-lotta-love-for-ludlow-led-zepplins-robert-plant-talks-about-his-time-in-the-town/|title=Whole Lotta Love for Ludlow! Led Zeppelin's Robert Plant talks about his time in the town|newspaper=[[Shropshire Star]] |date=7 February 2015 |access-date=1 August 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kidderminstershuttle.co.uk/news/14578642.Midlands_rock_god_Robert_Plant_cleared_of_stealing_Stairway_to_Heaven_riff/|title=Midlands rock god Robert Plant cleared of stealing Stairway to Heaven riff|newspaper=[[Kidderminster Shuttle]]|date=24 June 2016 |access-date=1 September 2017}}</ref> and is a member of Bewdley Tennis and Rowing Club(s).

12069472.title: Beningbrough Hall
12069472.extract:
Beningbrough Hall is a large Baroque mansion near the village of Beningbrough, North Yorkshire, England, and overlooks the River Ouse.
It has baroque interiors, cantilevered stairs, wood carving and central corridors which run the length of the house. Externally the house is a red-brick Baroque mansion with a grand drive running to the main frontage and a walled garden, The house is home to changing exhibitions on the first floor art gallery and stories of the estate on the ground floor. It has a restaurant, shop and garden shop, and was shortlisted in 2010 for the Guardian Family Friendly Museum Award.
The hall is set in extensive grounds and is separated from them by a ha-ha (a sunken wall) to prevent sheep and cattle entering the estate's gardens or the hall itself. The gardens are undergoing a redesign by garden designer Andy Sturgeon.

'''Beningbrough Hall''' is a large [[Baroque]]<ref name="NHLE">{{NHLE |desc=Beningbrough Hall, Beningbrough |num=1150998 |accessdate=7 May 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=History of Beningbrough Hall {{!}} Yorkshire |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/yorkshire/beningbrough/the-history-of-beningbrough-hall |access-date=7 May 2024 |website=National Trust }}</ref> mansion near the village of [[Beningbrough]], [[North Yorkshire]], [[England]], and overlooks the [[River Ouse, Yorkshire|River Ouse]].

It has [[baroque]] interiors, [[cantilevered stairs]], wood carving and central corridors which run the length of the house. Externally the house is a red-brick Baroque mansion with a grand drive running to the main frontage and a walled garden, The house is home to changing exhibitions on the first floor art gallery and stories of the estate on the ground floor. It has a restaurant, shop and garden shop, and was shortlisted in 2010 for the Guardian Family Friendly Museum Award.

The hall is set in extensive grounds and is separated from them by a [[ha-ha]] (a sunken wall)<ref>{{NHLE|num=1001057|desc=Beningbrough Hall|accessdate=26 September 2016}}</ref> to prevent sheep and cattle entering the estate's gardens or the hall itself. The gardens are undergoing a redesign by garden designer [[Andy Sturgeon]].

==History==
Beningbrough Hall, situated {{convert|10|km|order=flip}}<ref>{{cite map|title = York & Selby|map = 105|year = 1998 |scale =1:50,000 |series =Landranger |publisher =Ordnance Survey |edition = C|isbn =0-319-22407-4}}</ref>  north-west of [[York]], was built in 1716 by a York landowner, John Bourchier III<ref name="YP">{{cite news |editor-last1=Mitchinson |editor-first1=James |title=A Corner of Yorkshire: Beningbrough Water Tower |work=The Yorkshire Post |date=26 June 2021 |location=The Magazine |page=4|issn=0963-1496}}</ref> to replace his family's modest Elizabethan manor, which had been built in 1556 by Sir [[Ralph Bourchier]] on his inheritance to the estate.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hunt|first1=Abby|title=Beningbrough Hall, North Yorkshire; an archaeological survey and investigation of the Post-Medieval park and gardens|journal=English Heritage Research Department Report Series|date=2006|issue=79|page=3|publisher=English Heritage|issn=1749-8775}}</ref> Local builder William Thornton oversaw the construction, but Beningbrough's designer remains a mystery; possibly it was [[Thomas Archer]].{{sfn|Pevsner|2002|p=78}} Bourchier was [[High Sheriff of Yorkshire]] for 1719–1721 and died in 1736 at the age of 52.<ref name="TYP">{{cite news |title=Nostalgia on Tuesday. Hall of History |url=https://www.yorkshirepost.co.uk/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/nostalgia-tuesday-hall-history-1786904 |access-date=5 August 2022 |work=The Yorkshire Post |date=29 November 2016}}</ref>

[[File:CS p5.356 - Beningbrough Hall, Yorkshire - Morris's County Seats, 1880.jpg|thumb|left|Beningbrough Hall by [[Alexander Francis Lydon]] (1880)]]
John Bourchier (1710–1759) followed his father as owner of Beningbrough Hall and was High Sheriff in 1749. It then passed to Dr. Ralph Bourchier, a  71-year-old physician and from him to his daughter, Margaret, who lived there for 70 years. Today a [[Bourchier knot]] is cut into a lawn adjoining the house.<ref>[http://www.yorkshirelife.co.uk/homes-gardens/gardens/look_for_inspiration_in_the_kitchen_gardens_at_beningbrough_hall_near_york_1_1638280 "Look for inspiration in the kitchen gardens at Beningbrough Hall, near York"], ''Yorkshire Life'' magazine, 23 May 2010. Retrieved 1 December 2013</ref>

After over 100 years in the Bourchiers' possession, the estate passed in 1827 to the [[William Dawnay, 6th Viscount Downe|Rev. William Henry Dawnay]], the future 6th Viscount Downe, a distant relative.<ref name="YP"/> He died in 1846 and left the house to his second son, Payan, who was High Sheriff for 1851.<ref>{{cite ODNB|first=Richard|last=Davenport-Hines|title=Dawnay, Guy Payan|id=45721|date=23 September 2004}}</ref> The house was neglected, prompting fears that it might have to be demolished. In 1916, however, a wealthy heiress, [[Enid Scudamore-Stanhope, Countess of Chesterfield]], bought it and immediately set about its restoration, filling it with furnishings and paintings from her husband's ancestral home, [[Holme Lacy]] in [[Herefordshire]].<ref name="TYP"/>
[[File:Rear facade of Beningbrough Hall.jpg|left|thumb|Rear facade of Beningbrough Hall]]
During the Second World War the hall was occupied by the [[Royal Air Force]] then latterly, the [[Royal Canadian Air Force]], when under [[No. 6 Group RCAF|No. 6 Group]] of [[Bomber Command]], they took over some of the bases in the region (such as the nearby [[RAF Linton-on-Ouse]] and [[RAF Leeming]]).<ref>{{cite web|title=HISTORY IS MADE AT LINTON AS 426 (THUNDERBIRD) SQN RETURN TO BASE|url=http://www.raf.mod.uk/raflintononouse/newsweather/index.cfm?storyid=57DDED8E-5056-A318-A86C52455008D49C|website=RAF Linton-on-Ouse|accessdate=26 September 2016}}</ref>

Lady Chesterfield died in 1957, and in June 1958 the estate was acquired by the [[National Trust]] after it had been [[Acceptance in lieu|accepted by the government in lieu of death duties]] at a cost of £29,250.<ref>National Trust Beningbrough Hall Guidebook</ref> Initially, following the acquisition, the National Trust sought, unsuccessfully, to let the premises out for £1 per week.<ref>National Trust, public information notice on site, accessed 14 February 2026</ref>

In partnership with the [[National Portrait Gallery (United Kingdom)|National Portrait Gallery]] the hall now exhibits more than a hundred 18th-century portraits<ref>{{cite news|title=A walk on the outskirts of York: Beningbrough, North Yorkshire|url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2012/may/12/beninbrough-north-yorkshire-walk|accessdate=26 September 2016|work=The Guardian|date=12 May 2012}}</ref> and has seven new interpretation galleries called 'Making Faces: 18th-century Style'. Outside the main building there is a [[Victorian era|Victorian]] laundry and a [[walled garden]] with fruit and vegetable planting, the produce from which is used by the walled garden restaurant.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Barnet |first1=Ben |title=Historic garden set for bumper apple harvest |work=The Yorkshire Post |date=3 October 2013 |page=9|issn=0963-1496}}</ref>

Beningbrough Hall includes a wilderness play area, [[community orchard]], an [[Italy|Italianate]] border and garden shop. It hosts events, activity days, family art workshops,<ref>{{cite web|title=Family days out at Beningborough Hall|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/beningbrough-hall/features/family-days-out-at-beningbrough|publisher=National Trust|accessdate=26 September 2016}}</ref> and an annual food and craft festival which in 2010 was a Big Green Festival.<ref>[http://www.yorkpress.co.uk/news/8409646.Beningbrough_Hall_bedding_down_for_Big_Green_Festival/ "Beningbrough Hall bedding down for Big Green Festival"], ''The Press'', 23 September 2010. Retrieved 1 December 2013</ref>

==Architecture==
[[File:Haha at Beningbrough Hall.jpg|thumb|left|The ha-ha at Beningbrough Hall gardens]]
===House===
The house is built of red brick with stone dressings, [[quoin (architecture)|quoin]] strips, floor bands, paired [[console (architecture)|console]] brackets, a deep [[molding (architecture)|moulded]] [[cornice]] and blocking course, and a [[hip roof|hipped]] [[Westmorland]] [[slate]] roof.  There are two storeys, a basement and attics, a double pile plan, fronts of eleven and five [[bay (architecture)|bays]], and screen walls linking to [[pavilion]]s.  On the main front, the middle three bays project, and in the centre steps with an iron [[balustrade]] lead up to a doorway with an [[architrave]], [[Doric order|Doric]] [[pilaster]]s, and an [[entablature]] with a cornice, over which is a decorated [[cartouche (design)|cartouche]].  The windows are [[sash window|sashes]] with gauged brick arches.  The screen walls contain [[niche (architecture)|niches]] and balustrades.  The pavilions have two storeys and fronts of a single bay, and each contains angle pilasters, round arches with [[impost (architecture)|imposts]] and [[keystone (architecture)|keystones]], flat-arched windows, and a [[dentil]]led cornice. On the roof is a [[cupola]] with an [[ogee]] lead roof and a ball and spire [[finial]]; the left pavilion has a bell, and the right pavilion has a wind clock.  At the rear, the central doorway has channelled quoins, attached [[Ionic order|Ionic]] columns, a [[frieze]] and a cornice, above which is a cartouche and a segmental [[pediment]].<ref name="NHLE"/><ref name="pevsner">{{cite book| last1 =Grenville| first1 =Jane| last2 = Pevsner | first2 = Nikolaus | author2-link = Nikolaus Pevsner | series= The Buildings of England| title =Yorkshire: The North Riding| publisher =[[Yale University Press]] | year =2023 | orig-year=1966 |location =New Haven and London | isbn =978-0-300-25903-2 }}</ref>

===Stable Block===
[[File:The stables, Beningbrough Hall - geograph.org.uk - 4542734.jpg|thumb|right|The Stable Block]]
The grade II-listed Stable Block was built in the mid-18th century.  It is built of brick, with stone dressings, floor bands, stepped [[eaves]], and [[hip roof|hipped]] [[Westmorland]] [[slate]] roofs.  There are two storeys and a U-shaped plan, with a main range of seven [[bay (architecture)|bays]], and side wings of three bays.  The middle three bays of the main range project under a [[pediment]] containing an [[oeil-de-boeuf]] in the [[tympanum (architecture)|tympanum]].  In the ground floor is an [[arcade (architecture)|arcade]] of three round arches with [[impost (architecture)|imposts]], above which are three windows and a [[cornice]] on paired brackets, and on the roof is a [[cast iron]] [[wind vane]].  The outer bays contain round-arched doorways with [[fanlight]]s and windows, and in the upper floor are [[sash window]]s with segmental heads.  The wings contain segmental-headed carriage entrances.<ref>{{NHLE |num= 1151004|desc= Stable Block to North of Kitchen Garden, Beningbrough|access-date= 21 February 2024}}</ref><ref name="pevsner" />

===Norton Lodge===
[[File:Gateway to Beningborough Hall, Newton-on-Ouse.jpg|thumb|right|Norton Lodge]]
Norton Lodge, at the entrance to the grounds, is a late-18th century grade II-listed building.  It is built of stone and has a central round-arched gateway on a [[plinth]], with an [[impost (architecture)|impost]] bands extending as [[cornice]]s, an [[archivolt]] with a [[keystone (architecture)|keystone]] carved as a head, and flowers in the [[spandrel]]s. Above it is a corniced [[pediment]] with a laurel wreath in the [[tympanum (architecture)|tympanum]]. The gates are in [[cast iron]]. The archway is flanked by single-storey single-bay lodges containing a [[sash window]]. On the inner return is a doorway with a plinth, [[pilaster]]s, a cornice and a blocking course. Flanking the lodges are low [[coping (architecture)|coped]] walls with end [[pier (architecture)|piers]] and capstones, and cast iron railings with spear [[finial]]s.<ref name="pevsner" /><ref>{{NHLE |num=1190659|desc=Newton Lodge (entrance to Beningbrough Park), Newton-on-Ouse|access-date=14 July 2025}}</ref>

12751955.title: Hawford
12751955.extract:
Hawford is a hamlet in Worcestershire, England, located in the outer suburbs of Worcester, about 3 miles (4.8 km) from the city centre.
It falls within two parishes, North Claines and Ombersley. It is bisected by the River Salwarpe and the Droitwich-Worcester Canal, and is also bounded by the River Severn.

'''Wichenford''' is a village and civil parish (with [[Kenswick, Worcestershire|Kenswick]])  in the [[Malvern Hills (district)|Malvern Hills District]] in  the county of [[Worcestershire]], England. It lies  7 miles (11 km) to the north-west of the city of [[Worcester, England|Worcester]] and has a population of c 400 for around 250 households. Primary education is provided at nearby [[Hallow, Worcestershire|Hallow]], and at [[Martley]], which also has a secondary school.<ref>{{cite web
|url=https://kenswick-wichenford-pc.org.uk/index.php/parish-council/wichenford
|title=Kenswick and Wichenford Parish Council
|work=Wichenford
|publisher=Kenswick and Wichenford Parish Council
|accessdate=29 March 2021}}</ref> The civil parish population was 606 in 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wichenford |url=https://www.citypopulation.de/en/uk/westmidlands/admin/malvern_hills/E04010350__wichenford/ |website=City population |access-date=16 May 2026}}</ref>

==History==
{{See also|History of Worcestershire}}
[[File:WashbourneMonument StLawrence'sChurch WichenfordWorcs.jpg|thumb|left|[[Washburn (surname)|Washbourne]] monument at St Laurence's Wichenford]]
Two [[Roman Empire|Roman]] coins were found in the parish of Wichenford during an excavation at Woodend Farm which took place a few years before 1848. The coins are from the times of [[Victorinus]] and [[Constantinian dynasty|Constans]] of the early 4th century.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 1.</ref>

The name Wichenford probably derives from the [[Old English]] ''wiceford'' meaning '[[Ulmus glabra|wych elm]] [[ford (crossing)|ford]]'.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://kepn.nottingham.ac.uk/map/place/Worcestershire/Wichenford|title=Wichenford |website=Key to English Place-Names |publisher=The Institute for Name-Studies |access-date=18 November 2025}}</ref>

During the [[Anglo-Saxons|Anglo-Saxon]] period, Wichenford was gifted by [[Offa of Mercia]] (The Midland King) to the Church of Worcester in the later part of the 8th century.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 3.</ref>

A church or chapel has existed at Wichenford from early times with mention of a chapel which was attached to the church of [[Helena, mother of Constantine I|St. Helen]], Worcester around 1234. Parts of the present church of [[Saint Lawrence|St. Lawrence]] date from about 1320.<ref>[http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=43174 A History of the County of Worcester: Vol. 3 (1913)] Retrieved 24 May 2009</ref>

===Wichenford Court and Manor===
[[File:Wichenford Dovecote - geograph.org.uk - 4306847.jpg|thumb|left|Inside Wichenford Dovecote]]
The manor of Wichenford belonged to the [[Washburn (surname)|Washbourne or Washburn]] family, and there are two monuments with effigies and family heraldry in the church. The estate came into the Washbourne family from Margaret le Poher (d. 1454) who married John Washbourne, and her sister Agnes married another landowner in the village James de Habingdon.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 20.</ref>

It is said that around the year 1400, this Margaret Washbourne stabbed a French prisoner to death in Wichenford Court or ordered his execution,<ref>Edith Ophelia Browne & John Richard Burton,  ''Short Biographies of Worthies of Worcestershire'' (Worcester, 1916), p. 134.</ref> following a battle fought a few miles north of Wichenford on [[Woodbury Hill]] between forces loyal to [[Henry IV of England]] and [[Owain Glyndŵr]] from Wales who was supported by a contingent of French troops. A captured French nobleman was brought to Wichenford Court where he was murdered, a story which has persisted through the centuries, and there is allegedly still a bloodstain on the landing of the Court from the stabbed French gentleman.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 21.</ref> According to Robert Peach's 1896 history of the Washbourne family, the prisoner was one of the [[House of Bourbon|Bourbon Princes]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Peach |first=Robert Edward Myhill |year=1896 |title=The Washbourne Family: Notes And Records, Historic And Social of The Ancient Family of Washbourne of Washbourne, Wichenford and Pytchley From The 12th Century to The Present Time |url=https://archive.org/details/washbournefamily00peac/page/n9/mode/2up |location=Gloucester |publisher=[[John Bellows]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/washbournefamily00peac/page/n119/mode/2up 88] |access-date=June 29, 2022}}</ref>

In 1651, John Washbourne of Wichenford arrived at [[Pitchcroft]] in Worcester with "forty horse" to support [[Charles II of England]]. Although it is not clear what happened to him, he may have been killed at the subsequent [[Battle of Worcester]] as there is no reference to him after that and his wife was recorded as a [[widow]] in 1653.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 26.</ref>

Wichenford Court, a partly moated manor house, has a timber-framed 17th-century [[dovecote]], with 557 nesting boxes,<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 89.</ref> now in the care of the [[National Trust]].<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wichenford-dovecote 'Wichenford Dovecote', National Trust]</ref> 17th-century panelling from Wichenford Court was removed to decorate Kenswick Manor by the Britten family in 1895. Blanche Cecile Britten, a daughter of [[Charles Colville, 1st Viscount Colville of Culross]], and Rear-Admiral Richard Britten, resided at Kenswick and endowed several charitable foundations.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), p. 82.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Peach |first=Robert Edward Myhill |year=1896 |title=The Washbourne Family: Notes And Records, Historic And Social of The Ancient Family of Washbourne of Washbourne, Wichenford and Pytchley From The 12th Century to The Present Time |url=https://archive.org/details/washbournefamily00peac/page/n9/mode/2up |location=Gloucester |publisher=[[John Bellows]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/washbournefamily00peac/page/n35/mode/2up 9] |access-date=June 29, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Davenport |first=James |year=1907 |title=The Washbourne Family of Little Washbourne and Wichenford in the County of Worcester |location=London |publisher=[[Methuen Publishing|Methuen & Company]] |page=193}}</ref>

Wichenford Court and its grounds were restored after 1969, when the last tenant farmer, Mr Pugh, was fatally injured in an accident at work. This prompted the owner Lt. Col. Patrick Britten and his wife Elizabeth to decide to live in the house as their main residence.<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), pp. 36–37.</ref>

===1961 air incident===
On the evening of 7 February 1961, [[BAC Jet Provost]] 'XF893', from [[RAF Tern Hill]] in [[Shropshire]], hit a tree, and skidded across the road to [[Martley]].

23 year old Abbas Masry, of the [[Lebanese Air Force]], was killed.  It was his first solo flight, at night.<ref>''Birmingham Daily Post'' Wednesday 8 February 1961, page 26</ref><ref>''Staffordshire Sentinel'' Wednesday 8 February 1961, page 7</ref><ref>[https://asn.flightsafety.org/wikibase/145209 XF893]</ref><ref>[https://www.macearchive.org/films/midlands-news-08021961-aircraft-crash ATV report 1961]</ref>

In August 1960 he had been banned from driving, for one month, by [[Market Drayton]] Magistrates, for taking a bend at 50mph, hitting a hedge, and somersaulting. He had only five hours previous driving on British roads.<ref>''Staffordshire Sentinel'' Friday 26 August 1960, page 5</ref>

==Community==
Following the [[Poor Law Amendment Act 1834]] Wichenford Parish ceased to be responsible for maintaining the poor in its parish. This responsibility was transferred to [[Martley Poor Law Union]].<ref>Vanessa Morgan, ''Worcestershire Family History Guidebook'' (History Press: Stroud, 2011), p. 68.</ref>

Wichenford School, now closed, was founded by the landowner Skynner G. Woodroffe in 1847 and a new building erected in 1848 was augmented around the year 1875.<ref>Beach, A.J and Beach, E.M (1979). pp. 95–96.</ref>

The Wichenford branch of the [[Women's Institute]] was started in 1944.<ref>Beach, A.J and Beach, E.M (1979). p. 121.</ref> In the 1950s, the parish council arranged for Queen's Estate to be constructed and to make sure that the residents were able to park their cars.<ref>Beach, A.J and Beach, E.M (1979). p. 117.</ref>

Wichenford parish was joined with Kenswick parish, which had its own chapel, in 1972 for local government arrangements.<ref>Beach, A.J and Beach, E.M (1979). p. 118.</ref> In 1973, the parish council erected a bus shelter near Castle Hill and installed the first street lighting in the village which was at Queen's Estate.<ref>Beach, A.J and Beach, E.M (1979). p. 123.</ref>

== No Shops==
Until the mid-1990s Wichenford had both a village shop with Post Office and a village bakery, both now closed down. The two shops were situated at opposite sides of the village green, in the centre of the village. Wichenford also has a pub, the Mason's Arms, which is situated on the road to [[Martley]] and is not near the village centre.

==Village Hall==
Wichenford Memorial Hall  stands opposite the church and is used by local societies and for a variety of functions. The hall has modern kitchen facilities and a "committee room" with a bar area.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20120425140036/http://www.wichenfordhall.btck.co.uk/ Memorial Hall]}}</ref>

There is a "War Memorial" plaque within the hall to those from the village that have lost their lives while serving their country.

==Open Gardens and Village Fete==
Every two years (the "odd" years) a number of the village's gardens are opened by their owners over a weekend in June. The 2017 event made in excess of £10,000. Proceeds go to local charities. In even numbered years, a Fete is held in mid-July at The Memorial Hall. This popular event raises very welcome funds which are distributed to local good causes.<ref>[http://wichenfordopengardens.webplus.net/ Open Gardens]  Retrieved 8 August 2009</ref>

==Millennium Green==
In the year 2000 the [[Millennium Green]] was opened.

==In fiction==
Julius Falconer's 2010 publication ''The Wichenford Court Murder'' is an entirely [[fiction]]al story set in the 20th century and has no connection or coverage of the murder at Wichenford Court that took place in the early 1400s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Falconer |first=Julius |year=2010 |title=The Wichenford Court Murder |location=[[Dartford]], Kent |publisher=Pneuma Spring Publishing |page=inside cover (preface) |isbn=9781907728037}}</ref>

==Notable residents==
* [[Thomas Washbourne]] (1606–1687), poet<ref>Arthur J. Beach & E. Margery Beach, ''The Story of Wichenford'' (Upton-upon-Severn, 1979), pp. 20-21: R. E. Peach, ''The Washbourne Family'' (Gloucester, 1896), p. 8.</ref>
* [[Charles Colville, 5th Viscount Colville of Culross]], lived for at time at Abingdon Cottage

30612883.title: Rosedene
30612883.extract: Rosedene is a cottage built as part of the Great Dodford Chartist settlement. It is the best preserved example of a Chartist cottage built by the National Land Company is a listed building, and is owned by the National Trust.

main.*:
{{Short description|Chartist house and museum in Worcestershire, England}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
{{Use British English|date=February 2023}}
[[File:'Rosedene' Chartists Cottage, Dodford - geograph.org.uk - 1777279.jpg|thumb|Rosedene Dodford]]
'''Rosedene''' is a cottage built as part of the [[Dodford, Worcestershire|Great Dodford]] [[Chartism|Chartist]] settlement. It is the best preserved example of a Chartist cottage built by the [[National Land Company]]<ref name="nationaltrustarch">[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-ar_d_land.pdf Land for the landless, and votes for the disenfranchised. ''The history and archaeology of Rosedene, a surviving Chartist cottage. at Dodford with Grafton'', Shona Robson, in National Trust Annual Archaeological Review 1999-2000] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629105739/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-ar_d_land.pdf |date=2011-06-29 }}</ref> is a [[listed building]],<ref>[http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-156368-rose-dene-dodford-with-grafton Rose Dene, Dodford With Grafton, British Listed Buildings]</ref> and is owned by the [[National Trust]].<ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/rosedene Rosedene Cottage, National Trust]</ref>

==History and usage==

The cottage was built on Plot 29 of the settlement, and was bought by William Hodgkin. He paid £120 as a “bonus” (deposit discounting future ground rents) to secure the property, and another £130 to buy out the property from ground rent when the National Land Company was dissolved. This is the largest amount paid for a plot in a Chartist village.<ref name="nationaltrustarch" />

The original building had two bedrooms, a living room, dairy, store, back hall with well and pump, plus an adjoining piggery, coal house and privy.<ref name="nationaltrustarch" />

Alterations were made to the cottage. A stable was added before 1889, to help carry market garden produce (strawberries, pears and plums) to market in Birmingham. The piggery was converted to a laundry some time between 1915–20, probably as keeping pigs was less necessary as the village’s market garden economy was reasonably profitable. Alterations were made in the 1930s to include an extra bedroom in place of the old store and a new kitchen where the laundry room was, as well as new sitting room where the dairy had once been.<ref name="nationaltrustarch" />

==Restoration==
The building was bought by the [[National Trust]] in 1997. A donation of £1,000 was made by the [[Bromsgrove Society]] in 1999.<ref>[http://www.bsoc.co.uk/pdf/June2003.pdf Where Did That Money Go? Rosedene Restoration Fund, by Gordon Long, Bromsgrove Society Newsletter June 2003] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728174926/http://www.bsoc.co.uk/pdf/June2003.pdf |date=2011-07-28 }}</ref>

The cottage was restored to its original state by the Trust and was helped by long-time resident Mrs Florence Crane. The Trust retains a recording of her recollections of living in the property in their archives.

Rosedene now includes an organic garden<ref name="officialpage">[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-rosedene Rosedene, National Trust] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081122042759/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-rosedene |date=2008-11-22 }}</ref> and retains its plum and pear orchards.<ref name="nationaltrustarch" /> Tours can be made on the first Sunday of the month, between 6 March and 4 December by appointment, or otherwise by arrangement.<ref name="officialpage" />

39085731.title: Blakey Topping standing stones
39085731.extract:
Blakey Topping standing stones is a small group of standing stones near the Hole of Horcum in the North York Moors. It sits at the foot of Blakey Topping hill.
There are at least four standing stones currently surviving in this group, although some of them are of uncertain status. The tallest stone is 1.9 metres high and is much-weathered and leaning. A second stone is 1.0 metres high and appears to have had its top broken off. A third stone is 1.3 metres high but has been roughly squared off and is currently being used as a gate post. A fourth stone, 1.4 metres high, is found in an old field bank and is much-weathered and leaning. A fifth standing stone may exist, and two or three hollows in the ground may indicate the former position of other stones.
The stones may be the remains of a stone circle of about 17 metres in diameter. Alternatively, the stones may have formed part of a curving alignment or possibly two parallel rows.

There are at least four standing stones currently surviving in this group, although some of them are of uncertain status. The tallest stone is 1.9 metres high and is much-weathered and leaning. A second stone is 1.0 metres high and appears to have had its top broken off. A third stone is 1.3 metres high but has been roughly squared off and is currently being used as a gate post. A fourth stone, 1.4 metres high, is found in an old field bank and is much-weathered and leaning. A fifth standing stone may exist, and two or three hollows in the ground may indicate the former position of other stones.<ref name="pastscape">{{PastScape|num=63004 |desc=|accessdate=7 November 2013}}</ref>

The stones may be the remains of a [[stone circle]] of about 17 metres in diameter. Alternatively, the stones may have formed part of a curving alignment or possibly two parallel rows.<ref name="pastscape"/>

45330941.title: Middle Littleton Tythe Barn
45330941.extract: Middle Littleton Tythe Barn, also known as Middle Littleton Tithe Barn, is a grade I listed 13th or 14th-century tithe barn in the village of Middle Littleton, near Evesham in Worcestershire. It is one of the largest and most notable tithe barns in England. The barn is constructed of a mixture of Blue Lias and Cotswold stones, with a stone tile roof. It was originally built for Evesham Abbey, which was the third largest abbey in England. It is now owned and operated by the National Trust.

'''Middle Littleton Tythe Barn''', also known as Middle Littleton Tithe Barn, is a grade I [[listed building|listed]] 13th or 14th-century [[tithe barn]] in the village of [[Middle Littleton]], near [[Evesham]] in Worcestershire. It is one of the largest and most notable tithe barns in England.<ref name=NT>{{cite web|title=Middle Littleton Tithe Barn|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/middle-littleton-tithe-barn/|accessdate=7 February 2015}}</ref> The barn is constructed of a mixture of [[Blue Lias]] and [[Cotswold stone|Cotswold]] stones, with a stone tile roof.<ref name=listed>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1350092 |accessdate=4 April 2015}}</ref> It was originally built for [[Evesham Abbey]], which was the third largest abbey in England.<ref name="listed" /> It is now owned and operated by the [[National Trust]].

==History==
There is some uncertainty about when the barn was built. The National Trust describes it as 13th-century, whereas English Heritage describe it as 14th-century;<ref name=NT/><ref name="listed" /> the discrepancy may be the result of a radiocarbon date of around 1250 conflicting with evidence that the barn was built in 1376 by Abbot John Ombersley of Evesham Abbey.<ref name=Chilt>{{cite web|title=Middle Littleton Tithe Barn|url=http://www.chilternrailways.co.uk/station/lye/maps/detail/127920|accessdate=7 February 2015|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150207162353/http://www.chilternrailways.co.uk/station/lye/maps/detail/127920|archivedate=7 February 2015}}</ref>

The barn was built to hold [[tithes]] collected for Evesham Abbey, which was the third largest abbey in England before the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]]. The size of the barn is an indication of the importance of the abbey at this time.<ref name=BE>{{cite web|title=Middle Littleton Tithe Barn|url=http://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3668|accessdate=7 February 2015}}</ref> Also remaining from the [[Benedictine]] Evesham Abbey are two churches, a bell tower, a cloister arch and the [[Almonry Museum and Heritage   Centre|Almonry]].

==Architecture==
[[File:Middle Littleton Tithe Barn, Evesham, Worcestershire (3859488799).jpg|thumb|Middle Littleton Tithe Barn, Evesham, Worcestershire]]

The barn is constructed of Blue lias stone with Cotswold stone dressings. It has a triple [[purlin]] roof which is tiled in stone. The building has had several modifications; a pair of [[gable]]s on each side of the building were destroyed during the Victorian period and additions made to both sides. Smaller gables with ornate clover-leaf [[finials]] and many [[buttresses]] remain.<ref name="listed" />    

==Protection==
The barn was granted [[Grade I listed]] status on 30 July 1959.<ref name=listed />

==Operations==
The barn is owned by the National Trust and is open to the public.

'''Knowles Mill''' is the remains of an eighteenth-century water-powered grain mill, located in the [[Wyre Forest]] in Worcestershire, England. The mill has been owned by the [[National Trust]] since 1938. The mill and its surroundings feature extant machinery, as well as notable populations of [[Vipera berus|adders]] and [[Geranium sylvaticum|wood cranesbill]].

== Background ==
Knowles Mill is a Grade II listed water-powered [[Gristmill|grain mill]], located on [[Dowles Brook]], in the [[Wyre Forest]], [[Bewdley]], [[Worcestershire]].<ref name=":0">{{NHLE|num=1166692|desc=Knowles Mill|grade=II|access-date=31 July 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cherry |first=John |date=1 January 1972 |title=Post-Medieval Britain in 1971 |url=https://doi.org/10.1179/pma.1972.014 |journal=Post-Medieval Archaeology |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=208–223 |doi=10.1179/pma.1972.014 |issn=0079-4236|access-date=31 July 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last1=Halsted |first1=Jon |title=Knowles Mill, Wyre Forest, Bewdley, Worcestershire - Historic Building Recording, Archaeological Evaluation |last2=Hewitson |first2=Chris |last3=Booth |first3=Tim |publisher=Birmingham Archaeology |year=2010 |location=Birmingham |pages=14–22}}</ref> The forest is the UK's largest [[National nature reserve (United Kingdom)|National Nature Reserve]] and is administered by [[Forestry England]], [[Worcestershire Wildlife Trust]] and [[Natural England]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wyre Forest |url=https://www.forestryengland.uk/wyre-forest |access-date=26 July 2022 |website=Forestry England |language=en |archive-date=26 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726141215/https://www.forestryengland.uk/wyre-forest |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":5" /> However the mill, as well as the mill pond, meadow, cottage and gardens are National Trust property.<ref name=":5" />

The mill is approximately {{cvt|3/4|mi|m}} from the nearest car park.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Knowles Mill |url=https://www.spab.org.uk/mills/visit-a-mill/41778 |access-date=26 July 2022 |website=spab.org.uk |language=en |archive-date=17 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211017034037/https://www.spab.org.uk/mills/visit-a-mill/41778 |url-status=live }}</ref> The path to the mill roughly follows Dowles Brook stream.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boston |first=Irene |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FajYlrjUPM4C&dq=knowles+mill+national+trust&pg=PA16 |title=Best Tea Shop Walks in Worcestershire |date=1999 |publisher=Sigma Leisure |isbn=978-1-85058-646-3 |language=en |access-date=2022-07-27 |archive-date=2022-08-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811033849/https://books.google.com/books?id=FajYlrjUPM4C&dq=knowles+mill+national+trust&pg=PA16 |url-status=live }}</ref> The site also includes Knowles Mill Cottage, which is not accessible to the public.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1100006|desc=Knowles Mill Cottage|grade=II|access-date=31 July 2022}}</ref> The woodland Knowles Coppice surrounds the mill to the south.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Knowles Coppice {{!}} Worcestershire Wildlife Trust |url=https://www.worcswildlifetrust.co.uk/nature-reserves/knowles-coppice |access-date=26 July 2022 |website=www.worcswildlifetrust.co.uk |archive-date=26 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726141213/https://www.worcswildlifetrust.co.uk/nature-reserves/knowles-coppice |url-status=live }}</ref>

== History ==
One of nine possible mills that historically worked on Dowles Brook, Knowles Mill was built in the eighteenth century, and was later modified in the nineteenth century.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=MNA142413 National Trust Heritage Records |url=https://heritagerecords.nationaltrust.org.uk/HBSMR/MonRecord.aspx?uid=MNA142413 |access-date=26 July 2022 |website=heritagerecords.nationaltrust.org.uk}}</ref> The surviving building is two storeys high and the site also preserves an [[Water wheel|overshot mill wheel]] made of iron and a great spur wheel, alongside other remnant machinery.<ref name=":0" /> The first record of a mill on the site dates to 1757 when it was listed as for sale in a local newspaper.<ref name=":4" /> However there is documentary evidence preceding 1757 that lists owners of the land that the mill was built on. These owners include Arthur Palmer, c.1661, Edward Wheeler, c.1693, Roger Hunt, c.1704, Antony Betts, c.1717, Edward Faulkner, c.1722 and Daniel Crun, c.1735.<ref name=":5" />

The first owner of the mill was William Crun, in 1757. It passed through a number of owners, including William and Mary Herbert, William Nicholls and Arthur Nott.<ref name=":5" /> The mill takes its name from the Knowles family who worked there from 1803 to the 1870s; earlier names included Coventry Mill and Upper Town Mill.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Booth |first=Tim |date=2010 |title=Mills on Dowles Brook |url=http://wyreforest.net/wp-content/uploads/Historical_Articles/2010-Mills-on-Dowles-Brook_optimize.pdf |journal=Wyre Forest Study Group Annual Review |pages=10 |access-date=31 July 2022 |archive-date=8 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308143322/https://wyreforest.net/wp-content/uploads/Historical_Articles/2010-Mills-on-Dowles-Brook_optimize.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The first member of the family to be listed as owner was James Knowles.<ref name=":5" /> The mill continued in use until 1891, when it became no longer financially viable.<ref name=":1" />

It was donated to the [[National Trust]] by Paul Cadbury in 1938, along with four acres of orchards.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Matheson |first=Donald Macleod |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O4EpAQAAIAAJ&q=knowles+mill+national+trust |title=Places of Natural Beauty: National Trust Guide |date=1950 |publisher=Batsford |pages=66}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Airs |first=Malcolm |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f5kwAQAAIAAJ&q=knowles+mill+national+trust |title=The Twentieth Century Great House |date=2002 |publisher=Department for Continuing Education, Oxford University |isbn=978-0-903736-31-2 |pages=88}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> The property was visited by the historian [[James Lees-Milne]] during his work as a curator for the Trust.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lees-Milne |first1=James |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3fIEHXDK5toC&dq=%22knowles+mill%22&pg=PT76 |title=Diaries, 1942-1954 |last2=Bloch |first2=Michael |year=2011 |publisher=John Murray Press |isbn=978-1-84854-709-4 |access-date=2022-07-27 |archive-date=2022-08-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811033850/https://books.google.com/books?id=3fIEHXDK5toC&dq=%22knowles+mill%22&pg=PT76 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Archaeology ==
In 2010 [[Birmingham Archaeology]] investigated the site and found the remains of a cast iron mill wheel, as well as "remains of the head race culvert"; other trenches investigated water flow and the mill race.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> Artefacts from the excavations included a 17th-century [[yellowware]] pancheon bowl, a Sankey flowerpot, two shards of 18th-century green glass, an early 20th-century pocket-watch and a blue poison bottle inscribed "NOT TO BE TAKEN" from the wheel pit.<ref name=":5" /> There were 149 bottles or fragments of glass excavated from the site, representing brands such as Gartons HP Sauce, [[Bovril]], [[Kidderminster Brewery]], White Horse Distillers, Watville Dairies and Venos cough medicine.<ref name=":5" />

== Conservation ==
Since 1982, climatological measurements have been made at Knowles Mill and have been recorded and analysed at the [[University of Birmingham]].<ref name=":3">{{cite journal |last=Sheldon |first=Sylvia |url=https://wyreforest.net/wp-content/uploads/Reptiles%26Amphibian_Articles/2000-Reptiles-1999-SS2000_optimize.pdf |title=Wyre Forest Adder Census and Report 1999 and Adder Population Trends through the 1990s - Correlated with Meteorological Data |journal=Wyre Valley Study Group Annual Review |year=2011 |pages=35–39 |access-date=31 July 2022 |archive-date=19 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220619012941/http://wyreforest.net/wp-content/uploads/Reptiles%26Amphibian_Articles/2000-Reptiles-1999-SS2000_optimize.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The area surrounding the mill is notable for its [[Vipera berus|adder]] populations,<ref name=":3" /> and for the presence of [[Geranium sylvaticum|wood cranesbill]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bingham |first=John |url=https://wyreforest.net/wp-content/uploads/Flora_Articles/2003-JB-Uncommon-Plant-Species_optimize.pdf |title=Uncommon Plant Species found within the Wyre Forest |year=2003 |journal=Wyre Forest Study Group Annual Review |access-date=31 July 2022 |archive-date=8 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108143557/http://wyreforest.net/wp-content/uploads/Flora_Articles/2003-JB-Uncommon-Plant-Species_optimize.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>
